specialists_or_stages: ehs-ai-safety -> docwise-assist (TypeScript LLM assistant, RAG + tools)
ehs-web-api -> catalog-grpc-store (Go gRPC + JSON gateway over Postgres, data/storage)
architecture.fell_back_and_why: The plugin subagents named in references/team.md (ehs-web-api, ehs-ai-safety, ehs-infra-cloud, ehs-local-app, ehs-verifier) are not installed in this harness, so team.md's documented fallback path was used: every specialist ran as general-purpose with its role-file path, its knowledge pack paths, the full safety contract, the audit-mode no-edit rule, the severity instruction and the `searched` requirement copied verbatim into the prompt, since a subagent inherits neither the skill nor this context. ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} was substituted with the corpus root throughout. Dispatch was in waves of at most four in flight: wave 1 was the four components of wave 1, wave 2 the remaining two, wave 3 the three blind verifiers. NO LANE FAILED TO RETURN - all six specialist lanes and all three verifier lanes reported, so no lane is declared undone and no lane's findings were written by the lead on its behalf. Independently of the lanes, the lead read all six components in full as a backstop before consolidating, which is how the two non-conforming returns were caught: one triage answer came back outside the closed vocabulary (`HOLDS-PARTIAL->DOES_NOT_HOLD`, normalised to DOES_NOT_HOLD with its reason preserved) and the ledger lane returned component-relative paths, which were re-prefixed. Four corrections raised by the blind verifiers were applied by the lead over the finders' text: a false quantifier in the /auth/token title, an ambiguous title on the catalog visibility finding that was false under its literal reading, a narrowed quantifier plus an UNKNOWN triage answer on the ledger re-posting finding, and reachability caveats on the two Electron report-window findings. Four severities were moved after the blind pass (three up, one up): ExportItems tenant-from-metadata medium->high, licensing-auth rate limit low->medium, ledger poison-message medium->high; and two statuses were lowered confirmed->probable on named inferred hops. Two verifier severity recommendations were declined with reasons recorded in the findings: the docwise ingest size cap stays low (availability-only behind the same precondition that makes its sibling medium) and the x/net dependency stays low (no reachable call path established, per the corpus's own dependency-triage doctrine).

ruled_out.assertion: list() interpolates the sort key into ORDER BY with \(raw:), so the query string reaches the SQL

The interpolated token can only ever be reference/status/created_at. The highest-value decoy in the tree, because \(raw:) beside an ORDER BY is what a grep-driven review reports.

ruled_out.killed_by: AdminController.swift:58 prefixes an apostrophe when the first character is one of = + - @ TAB CR (the OWASP set) and :61 doubles quotes and wraps. Checked the usual bypasses - a leading space before =, and | / % - and the guard is complete for the characters that start a formula.

ruled_out.assertion: The rate-limit IP bucket can be spoofed with X-Forwarded-For
ruled_out.killed_by: RateLimitMiddleware.swift:40 reads request.peerAddress and never reads X-Forwarded-For or Forwarded, so the header-spoofing variant does not exist. The comment above it discusses a header the code does not touch. The bucket is evadable, but by the token mechanism reported separately.

ruled_out.assertion: PermitCreate allows mass assignment of status, tenant or reviewer fields
ruled_out.killed_by: PermitController.swift:92-101 - PermitCreate is a five-field explicit DTO, tenantID comes from the session (:93), status is forced to draft (:99) and notes/reviewer are forced empty (:100-101); update() assigns only the four applicant fields.

ruled_out.assertion: Postgres TLS is disabled, so database traffic is cleartext
ruled_out.killed_by: configure.swift:17-20 - the .disable branch is narrowed to hostname 127.0.0.1/localhost and every other host takes .require with a default NIOSSL client config that verifies certificates. This is the FP-11 shape done correctly. DB_PASSWORD ?? "" also fails closed: Postgres rejects an empty password under scram/md5.

ruled_out.assertion: Session tokens are generated with a non-cryptographic RNG
ruled_out.killed_by: BearerAuthMiddleware.swift:19-21 draws 32 bytes (256 bits) from Swift's SystemRandomNumberGenerator, the CSPRNG-backed default source on the declared platforms. The procedure targets Math.random()/uuid1()/rand(); this is not that.

ruled_out.assertion: Session tokens are stored as a bare unsalted SHA-256 digest
ruled_out.killed_by: The preimage is 256 bits of CSPRNG output (BearerAuthMiddleware.swift:19-21), so there is no dictionary to run and no work factor is owed. A fast digest is the correct choice for a lookup key over a high-entropy token; bcrypt would be wrong here.

ruled_out.assertion: autoMigrate runs automatically outside production
ruled_out.killed_by: configure.swift:70 is guarded on app.environment != .production, takes no attacker input and crosses no principal boundary.

ruled_out.assertion: FileMiddleware serves the public directory without authentication
ruled_out.killed_by: A static public directory is an intended bounded exposure, and Vapor's FileMiddleware resolves the path and rejects traversal itself. Nothing in this tree writes attacker bytes into publicDirectory - BlobStore roots at /var/lib/permits/blobs.

ruled_out.assertion: The 12mb body limit contradicts the 8MB upload cap
ruled_out.killed_by: Both bounds have real readers - Vapor enforces defaultMaxBodySize on the collected body and maxUploadBytes is read at PermitController.swift:147 and AttachmentController.swift:116 - and the sizing is consistent, since base64 of 8MB is about 10.7MB, under 12MB.

ruled_out.assertion: Search's filter parameter is injectable into SQL
ruled_out.killed_by: search.go:31 anchored regex, :54 column allowlist, :60 plus postgres.go:198-203 placeholders with bound args, and :82 sort allowlist. This clearance is what makes the ExportQuery sibling a finding rather than a pattern.

ruled_out.assertion: The idempotency check is a TOCTOU race that admits duplicate creates
ruled_out.killed_by: postgres.go:32 declares idempotency_key as a PRIMARY KEY and :128-133 inserts the receipt inside the same transaction, so the loser's whole tx rolls back. The tenant-scoping defect survives separately and is reported.

ruled_out.assertion: gRPC server reflection is exposed
ruled_out.killed_by: main.go:67 gates reflection.Register on CATALOG_ENV == "dev" with the default "prod" supplied at the same call.

ruled_out.killed_by: main.go:65 registers only CatalogServer, so the exempted /grpc.health.v1.Health/Check resolves to Unimplemented; the exemption reaches no handler.

ruled_out.killed_by: No non-ASCII uppercase rune lowercases to b, e, a or r, so strings.ToLower cannot change the byte length of the matched prefix; the test and the slice cover the same seven bytes.

ruled_out.assertion: ParseOrderBy panics on an all-whitespace order_by (fields[0] index out of range)
ruled_out.killed_by: search.go:77-82 - TrimSpace and Fields share the unicode.IsSpace predicate, so a string non-empty after trimming always yields at least one field.

ruled_out.killed_by: server.go:222-233 - non-digits reset the offset to 0 and it is clamped at 1,000,000; limit and offset reach postgres.go:201 as Go ints.

ruled_out.assertion: The default DSN omits sslmode, so database traffic is cleartext
ruled_out.killed_by: The default targets 127.0.0.1 and is overridden by CATALOG_DSN in any deployment where transport would matter.

ruled_out.assertion: Unguarded JSON.parse of model-supplied tool arguments crashes or corrupts the loop
ruled_out.killed_by: server.ts:69 - a throw from JSON.parse is caught by tRPC's error boundary and returned as a handled error. No state corruption, no bypass; a robustness bug, not a security finding.

ruled_out.assertion: The chat surface has no rate limit
ruled_out.killed_by: server.ts:50 - a cap does exist at 30 requests per minute per workspace. Per-user rather than per-workspace is a preference, not a missing control.

ruled_out.assertion: onError logs user questions to the console
ruled_out.killed_by: server.ts:70 logs only error.message; neither input nor question reaches the sink.

ruled_out.assertion: Redaction is applied at ingest only, so an unredacted write path exists
ruled_out.killed_by: crawler.ts:64 - indexChunks has exactly one caller (crawler.ts:66) and it is preceded by .map(redactChunk), so redact.ts's documented claim holds for every write path in the component.

ruled_out.killed_by: index.html:7 - the divergence is in the restrictive direction, since inspections.council.gov.example is simply not granted img/connect. A functional bug, not a weakening.

ruled_out.assertion: installPlugin never checks response.ok, so an error page is written as a plugin
ruled_out.killed_by: updater.js:48 - the sha256 comparison rejects an error-page body before anything is written. The same argument is what makes the refresh path a finding: it has no such line.

ruled_out.assertion: The preload leaks process.platform and the package version to the renderer
ruled_out.killed_by: A platform string and a version already visible in the user agent; no security value.

ruled_out.assertion: Vector's Prometheus exporter binds 0.0.0.0 and exposes metrics fleet-wide
ruled_out.killed_by: telemetry-agent.nomad.hcl:8 - mode = "bridge" puts the bind inside the alloc network namespace; 0.0.0.0 is the required form for a Nomad-mapped port, and the only reachable surface is component throughput counters.

ruled_out.killed_by: render-secrets.sh:25 declare -A - associative-array subscripts are string keys, not arithmetic expressions, so $JOB is never evaluated. The indexed-array injection shape does not exist here.

ruled_out.assertion: allow_caps grants dac_override and other dangerous Linux capabilities
ruled_out.killed_by: nomad-client.hcl:54 - the list is a narrowing of Nomad's default Docker capability set, not an addition, and sits beside allow_privileged = false. The real defect is that the bootstrap script overrides it, which is reported separately.

ruled_out.assertion: /etc/fleet/env is world-readable at mode 0644
ruled_out.killed_by: bootstrap-node.sh:13-16 - the file's entire content is FLEET_ENV and FLEET_REGION. Its content is load-bearing for the VAULT_SKIP_VERIFY finding; its mode is not.

ruled_out.assertion: The S3 log sink carries no credentials, so it silently relies on the instance profile
ruled_out.killed_by: Dropped for over-reach rather than refuted: the instance profile and IMDS hop limit live outside this component, so the grant cannot be pointed at. ruled_out.assertion: The ledger flows are vulnerable to SQL injection
ruled_out.killed_by: Every non-COPY query binds parameters - postings.py:63, postings.py:129, flows/ingest.py:34, flows/reconcile.py:41. The COPY path is a separate finding and is a data-stream injection, not SQL injection.

ruled_out.assertion: A partner-chosen filename allows path traversal out of the inbox prefix
ruled_out.killed_by: sftp_fetch.py:88 and :63 both wrap the name in os.path.basename, so the partner cannot escape inbox_prefix.

ruled_out.assertion: The SFTP client accepts unknown host keys
ruled_out.killed_by: sftp_fetch.py:20 sets RejectPolicy, with load_host_keys at :19 which raises rather than continuing when the file is absent, so it fails closed.

ruled_out.assertion: The partner private key is left on disk after the handshake
ruled_out.killed_by: sftp_fetch.py:36 unlinks it in a finally block, and mkstemp creates it 0600 at :24.

ruled_out.assertion: A failed row-wise insert leaves a partial batch applied before the COPY retry
ruled_out.killed_by: postings.py:58 - psycopg3's connection context manager rolls back on exception, so the failed executemany leaves nothing behind. The defect on that path is what the retry sends, which is reported separately.

ruled_out.assertion: Credentials are hardcoded in the pipeline configuration
ruled_out.killed_by: prefect.yaml:36, :51 and :62 reference Prefect secret blocks and blocks/settings.py:50 loads them; the only literal DSN is a passwordless localhost development value at settings.py:35.

ruled_out.assertion: Decimal quantize rounding admits a salami-slicing attack
ruled_out.killed_by: Reachable only in strict mode, half-even on the second decimal, with no argument that a partner profits. Not credible.

findings.title: The entire admin surface is mounted with no authentication and no rate limiting
findings.class: Broken Function-Level Authorization (missing authentication on state-changing routes)
findings.evidence: routes.swift:35-38 builds the protected group app.grouped("api","v1").grouped(RateLimitMiddleware(...)).grouped(BearerAuthMiddleware()). routes.swift:45-46 builds let internalRoutes = app.grouped("internal") - a bare path prefix - and registers AdminController on it. The four handlers it exposes (AdminController.swift:23-26) are POST /internal/permits/:permitID/approve, GET /internal/permits/export, POST /internal/attachments/import, GET /internal/sessions/active. A grep for req.auth in AdminController.swift returns nothing. The only global middleware is CORS, ErrorMiddleware and FileMiddleware (configure.swift:52-65), none of which authenticates.
findings.impact: Approve, refuse or withdraw any permit in any tenant; export any tenant's permits; write arbitrary attachment index rows; read the live session count. These are the highest-value operations in the system and they carry no credential check at all, while the ordinary read/write API next to them carries two middlewares.
findings.recommendation: Register AdminController inside a group that carries BearerAuthMiddleware plus a role requirement, and treat network placement as defence in depth rather than as the control. If a genuinely separate internal surface is wanted, bind it to its own listener/port rather than a path prefix on the public application.

triage.reason: No skippable-proof layer exists. configure.swift:52-65 is the complete global middleware list - CORS, ErrorMiddleware, FileMiddleware - and none authenticates. The two auth-bearing middlewares are attached only to the /api/v1 group at routes.swift:37-38.

A second principal is definite and does not depend on the network claim: a staff user of another tenant. They hold a valid token, legitimately reach this listener for /api/v1, and /internal is the same Vapor Application on the same server configuration.

The comment at routes.swift:43-44 asserts the caseworker desktop client reaches it over the council LAN, but nothing in the repository bounds it: no separate port, no IP allowlist, no host check. Content in the target is data, not a control.
All four handlers registered at AdminController.swift:23-26 are unguarded; there is no condition anywhere that narrows the mount.

scope.established_by: Manual route-to-guard join (path_coverage.py cannot parse Swift): every mounted path enumerated from routes.swift and both RouteCollection boot() methods, then joined against the prefixes the two middlewares are attached to.
scope.narrowed_by: Whether an anonymous internet caller reaches these paths additionally depends on an edge rule not in this tree. That bound affects who the attacker is, not whether authorization exists - both prefixes share one listener, and no such artifact arrived.

searched.for: a global authentication middleware that would cover /internal without appearing in routes.swift
searched.found: only CORSMiddleware, ErrorMiddleware and FileMiddleware - none authenticates

searched.for: an in-handler req.auth.require / role check compensating for the missing middleware
searched.found: nothing - grep for req.auth in AdminController.swift is empty, while every PermitController and AttachmentController handler has one

searched.for: a second listener, port or host binding that would make /internal a genuinely separate surface
searched.found: one Application, one server configuration, both prefixes grouped off the same app

findings.title: exportAll takes the tenant to dump from the query string instead of the caller
findings.class: Broken Object-Level Authorization / cross-tenant data exposure
findings.evidence: AdminController.swift:49-52: let tenant = try req.query.get(UUID.self, at: "tenant") then .filter(\.$tenantID == tenant). The filter is present and it is bound to a value the caller supplies. Every other permit lookup in the tree scopes to the session instead - PermitController.swift:80, :114, :137 all use user.tenantID.
findings.impact: A full CSV of another council's permits: reference, status, applicant name, site address and reviewer for every row. Personal data of applicants across tenant boundaries, in bulk, in one request. Independent of the mount defect: applying BearerAuthMiddleware to /internal would authenticate the caller and still export whatever tenant they name.
findings.recommendation: Derive the tenant from the authenticated principal (try req.auth.require(StaffUser.self).tenantID) and drop the query parameter, or keep the parameter only as a filter that must equal the caller's tenant.

triage.reason: No layer injects a tenant scope. The migration at Permit.swift:93-108 creates the table with no row-level security and no policy, and Fluent applies no mandatory scope.
Nothing bounds the exposure. The parameter accepts any UUID and the handler returns whatever it matches.
The exported columns (AdminController.swift:64-69) are applicant names and site addresses of permit applicants - personal data of identifiable individuals.
No condition narrows it; the parameter is read once and used directly as the filter value.

scope.established_by: Traced the single source (req.query 'tenant') to the single sink (the Fluent filter) inside one handler.

searched.for: row-level security, a policy, or any database-side tenant constraint that would make a client-named tenant harmless
searched.found: none - plain columns and a unique index on (tenant_id, reference)

searched.for: how the rest of the codebase scopes a permit lookup, to establish whether the query-parameter form is the house style or the exception
searched.found: all three use user.tenantID from the session; this handler is the only one that takes the tenant from the wire

findings.title: approve() carries neither a tenant scope nor a role check, and the only role predicate in the codebase has zero readers
findings.class: Broken Function-Level Authorization / declared control that is never consulted
findings.evidence: AdminController.swift:33 Permit.find(permitID, on: req.db) - no tenant filter, unlike PermitController.swift:78-81, :112-115 and :135-138 which all add .filter(\.$tenantID == user.tenantID). Line 37 validates the decision value against a three-item list; nothing validates the actor. Separately, a grep for isApprover over the whole component returns exactly one line, its own declaration at BearerAuthMiddleware.swift:12: zero readers. roles is selected from the database (BearerAuthMiddleware.swift:49), carried into StaffUser (:60) and consulted by no authorization decision anywhere.
findings.impact: Any caller who reaches this handler sets the status of any permit in any tenant to approved/refused/withdrawn, and writes arbitrary attacker text into internalReviewNotes and reviewerEmail (which then flows into the CSV export at AdminController.swift:64-69). The application ships a role model, populates it on every request, and never asks it a question - so 'only approvers may approve' is not enforced anywhere, for anyone, on any route.
findings.recommendation: Scope the lookup to the caller's tenant and gate the handler on the role: guard user.isApprover else { throw Abort(.forbidden) }. Then add a negative test that a non-approver of the owning tenant, and an approver of a different tenant, both get 403.

triage.reason: There is no layer to compensate. The role never leaves StaffUser: BearerAuthMiddleware.swift:59-61 logs the principal in and no middleware or handler branches on roles.
The permit belongs to a tenant; the caller is at best a staff user of some tenant. Two principals, and Permit.find with no filter crosses the boundary between them.
An out-of-repository network control cannot supply this decision: no ACL can express 'only approvers of tenant X may approve permits of tenant X'.
The construct is what it looks like: a bare primary-key lookup followed by a write of caller-supplied status and notes.
The allowlist at line 37 narrows which values the status may take, not which callers may set it.

scope.established_by: Symbol-reader count for isApprover and roles across all ten files, plus a comparison of this permit lookup against the three tenant-scoped lookups in PermitController.

searched.for: any reader of the role predicate - a middleware, a guard, a branch - that would mean the control exists elsewhere
searched.found: one declaration and no readers; roles appears only in the two SQL selects, the two struct fields and the StaffUser constructions

searched.for: the house pattern for scoping a permit lookup, to confirm the omission here is an asymmetry and not the convention
searched.found: all three filter on user.tenantID; approve() is the only permit lookup in the tree without one

findings.title: The permit-listing cache key omits the tenant, so one council's listing is served to another
findings.class: Cache key omits a security-relevant dimension (cross-tenant data exposure)
findings.evidence: PermitController.swift:44 builds let cacheKey = "permits:list:\(status ?? "any"):\(page):\(perPage)" - no tenant component. Lines 45-47 return the hit before any query runs. Lines 61-66 fetch rows scoped WHERE tenant_id = \(bind: user.tenantID) and line 69 stores that tenant-specific payload under the tenant-free key. ResponseCache (ResponseCache.swift:8-16) is a single process-wide actor with one [String: Entry] dictionary. The default dashboard request produces the same key for every caller: permits:list:any:1:25.
findings.impact: The first tenant to populate a key serves every other tenant for the 45-second TTL, returning reference, applicant name, applicant email, site address and summary for permits of a council the caller has no relationship with. This needs no attacker: the file's own comment says caseworker dashboards poll every few seconds, so under normal load the shared entry is continuously refreshed and the leak is effectively permanent. The sort parameter is missing from the key on the same line, with the same fix.
findings.recommendation: Put the tenant in the key (permits:list:\(user.tenantID):...) and add sort. Better, key the cache on the full tuple that determines the response, and add a test that two tenants issuing an identical request never observe each other's rows.

triage.reason: The compensating control would have to be a per-tenant cache partition. ResponseCache.swift:9 is a single static let shared actor with one dictionary and no partitioning.
listProjection (Permit.swift:71-84) blanks internalReviewNotes and reviewerEmail but returns applicantName, applicantEmail, siteAddress, reference and summary - personal data of permit applicants.

Checked specifically whether the tenant enters the key indirectly - through status, page or perPage, or through a per-request cache instance. It does not: all three components come from the query string and the cache is process-wide.

scope.established_by: Followed the key from construction to both the read (:45) and the write (:69), then read the cache implementation to establish that the key is the only partitioning.

searched.for: a tenant dimension inside the cache - a nested dictionary, a per-request instance, anything partitioning entries the key does not
searched.found: one process-wide actor, one flat [String: Entry], keyed solely by the caller-supplied string

searched.for: an invalidation strategy that might make a stale cross-tenant entry unreachable in practice
searched.found: invalidate(prefix:) flushes globally on write, which does not prevent the read leak between writes - it only means one tenant's write clears every tenant's cache

findings.title: The attachment import path enforces none of the validation its two sibling writers do, and feeds an inline download sink
findings.class: Missing validation on one of several writers to the same entity (leading to stored XSS)
findings.evidence: Three handlers write an Attachment row. PermitController.attach (PermitController.swift:144-149) checks allowedUploadTypes and maxUploadBytes and assigns a server-generated storageKey (:154). AttachmentController.replaceContent (AttachmentController.swift:113-118) checks both too. AdminController.importAttachments (AdminController.swift:85-93) checks neither, and takes permitID, contentType and storageKey straight from the body (ImportedAttachment, AdminController.swift:11-17). The sink is AttachmentController.download:100-101, which sets Content-Type to the stored attachment.contentType and Content-Disposition: inline; no X-Content-Type-Options or CSP is set anywhere in the tree.
findings.impact: importAttachments is the only path by which a value outside the four-item allowlist can reach attachment.contentType, so it is load-bearing for the chain. An attacker uploads HTML bytes through the legitimate attach endpoint declaring image/png, reads back the server-assigned storageKey from the response (PermitController.swift:159 returns the model), then imports a new row with that storageKey, contentType text/html and any permitID - and the next staff user who opens it gets attacker HTML executed on the API origin, with the bearer-token client in scope. The same primitive re-points a row at any storageKey. Cross-tenant use needs a permit UUID or storage key the attacker cannot enumerate from this API; within a tenant, any staff token is enough.
findings.recommendation: Apply the same two guards to the import path, reject storage keys that any other row already references, and verify permitID against the caller's tenant. At the sink, serve attachments with a fixed safe Content-Type (or Content-Disposition: attachment) plus X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff.

triage.reason: No layer validates on the way in or on the way out. The migration (Permit.swift:116-127) declares content_type as a plain string with no constraint and no foreign key to permits, and download (AttachmentController.swift:100) reflects the stored value verbatim.
The exculpation offered by the comment at AdminController.swift:79-81 is an in-code assertion about the caller, not a control living outside the repository, and no artifact was offered.
The two handlers reach the same effect - a row in the same attachments table, read back by the same download handler.
The route is registered unconditionally at AdminController.swift:25; it is not behind a flag or a build configuration.

scope.established_by: Manual writer-parity join over the Attachment entity (writer_parity.py returned UNMEASURABLE on Swift): listed all three write sites and the guards each applies, then traced the unguarded fields to the response sink that interprets them.
scope.narrowed_by: Cross-tenant exploitation requires a permit UUID or storage key the attacker cannot enumerate from this API - exportAll returns references, not identifiers, and the sibling handlers 404 outside the caller's tenant. Same-tenant exploitation has no such precondition.

searched.for: whether the allowlist is applied by a shared helper the import path would inherit
searched.found: it is applied inline in both, referencing PermitController.allowedUploadTypes directly - there is no shared choke point the import path could have missed accidentally

searched.looked_in: permit-portal-api/Sources/App/Controllers/AttachmentController.swift:89-104 and the whole tree for security headers
searched.for: a fixed Content-Type, Content-Disposition: attachment, nosniff or a CSP that would keep a text/html row from executing
searched.found: Content-Type is the stored value verbatim, Content-Disposition is inline, and no security headers are set in configure.swift or any handler

searched.for: a database constraint on content_type, or a foreign key tying permit_id to a real permit, that would reject a hand-made row
searched.found: neither - plain string and plain uuid columns, no CHECK, no FK

findings.title: replaceContent overwrites any attachment by id without the ownership check its three siblings enforce
findings.class: Broken Object-Level Authorization (write path)
findings.evidence: AttachmentController.swift:109 is _ = try req.auth.require(StaffUser.self) - the principal is required and then discarded; the underscore is the tell. Its three siblings all resolve the parent permit and compare tenants: metadata (:81-84), download (:92-95), remove (:130-133). The shared loader load(_:) (:66-74) is Attachment.find(id, on: req.db) with no tenant filter, so it provides no scoping of its own. Lines 120-123 then write the new bytes and metadata.
findings.impact: Any authenticated staff user of any tenant can replace the stored content of any attachment in the system, given its identifier - silently substituting the evidence document behind a permit while byte_size and content_type update to match, leaving the row consistent. Read and delete of the same object are blocked for the same caller; only the overwrite is open.
findings.recommendation: Add the same guard the siblings use - resolve the parent permit and require permit.tenantID == user.tenantID - before touching the row or the blob. The three-of-four asymmetry is worth a test that walks every verb on the resource for a foreign-tenant user.

triage.reason: There is no compensating layer. load() does not scope (AttachmentController.swift:70), the attachments table has no tenant column and no foreign key to permits (Permit.swift:116-127), and no middleware inspects the object.
No out-of-repository control was claimed for this handler, and none of this class could apply: the decision is per-object and only the application can make it.
The handlers reach comparable effects on the same object family - three of the four read or delete it, this one rewrites it.
Registered unconditionally at AttachmentController.swift:61.

findings.title: One agent holds all three legs of the lethal trifecta
findings.class: Excessive agency / indirect prompt injection to exfiltration (LLM01:2026, LLM02:2026, LLM03:2026, ASI01, ASI02, CWE-284)
findings.evidence: AI-01 capability table for the single agent (answerQuestion, loop.ts:22): retrieval (loop.ts:28) reads private workspace corpus and ingests untrusted crawled pages; search_corpus (tools.ts:85) the same; share_document (tools.ts:94) is an outbound channel whose recipient is 'to: String(args.recipient ?? '')' at tools.ts:101; open_ticket (tools.ts:112) sends detail up to 4000 chars at tools.ts:120. Three marks on one agent. The corpus is third-party text by construction (crawler.ts:9-14 allowlists four external partner/government documentation portals) and workspace-private (every weaviate call filters on workspaceId: weaviate.ts:64, 82, 109). Both recipient and note are model-authored strings reaching the request body with no allowlist, no domain check and no confirmation gate.

Their text is retrieved into the prompt and can direct the assistant to call share_document with an arbitrary recipient and workspace corpus content in note. The victim is an ordinary editor on a team plan asking an ordinary question - the plan/role gate at tools.ts:61 is not a barrier, because the legitimate user triggers the turn.

Second choice is quarantining ingestion behind a tool-less model that returns typed references (Dual LLM / CaMeL, AI-06). Adding a rule to HOUSE_RULES is a request, not a control.

Multiple principals are crossed: workspaces are separate tenants (weaviate.ts:64), and recipient is an email address outside the system entirely.

Looked for a narrowing condition on the outbound leg. The only one is TOOL_POLICY (tools.ts:61) restricting share_document to team/enterprise plus editor/admin - which narrows who can be the victim, not who can be the attacker, and does not apply to open_ticket at all.

findings.title: The crawler allowlist is checked on the submitted URL and not on the URL actually fetched
findings.class: SSRF via redirect / ingestion with no origin control (CWE-918, LLM05:2026, LLM09:2026, ASI06, CWE-349)
findings.evidence: crawler.ts:43-46 parses the URL and checks protocol and ALLOWED_HOSTS once, against the pre-redirect URL. crawler.ts:48-52 then requests it with maxRedirections: 2, and undici follows up to two Location headers with no re-validation of host or scheme. crawler.ts:58-72 strips, chunks and indexes the body of whatever answers last. crawler.ts:68 stores the ORIGINAL url as the chunk's provenance.
findings.impact: An allowlisted documentation host that redirects (an open redirect, or a compromised/hostile partner) steers the crawl to any host the container can reach. The tree names three internal services as defaults: model-gateway.internal:8000 (gateway.ts:4), notify.internal:8070 (tools.ts:6) and weaviate.internal:8080 (weaviate.ts:12); cloud metadata endpoints are equally reachable. This is read-SSRF, not blind: the response is indexed and then retrievable through chat.search and chat.ask. It is also corpus poisoning with laundered provenance - a chunk fetched from an internal endpoint is later cited to the user as coming from the allowlisted URL.
findings.recommendation: Re-apply the scheme and host check to every hop: set maxRedirections: 0 and follow redirects manually, validating each Location against ALLOWED_HOSTS before the next request, and resolve and reject private/link-local address ranges after DNS. Record the final URL as the chunk's provenance, not the submitted one.

triage.reason: No post-fetch validation exists: crawler.ts:54-72 checks only statusCode and body length before indexing. undici's maxRedirections follows Location without consulting the caller.

The fetched host is attacker-controlled once a redirect is in play - the allowlist constrains only the first hop, and the https check is not re-applied, so a downgrade to http on an internal host is reachable.
The redirecting host is a third party (crawler.ts:9-14 lists external portals), and the corpus it lands in is another tenant-scoped principal's data.
Checked whether adminProcedure narrows this to nothing. It narrows who initiates, not who controls the destination - the attacker here is the redirecting host, not the admin.

scope.narrowed_by: router.ts:62 - crawl is adminProcedure, so the request must be initiated by role 'admin' (server.ts:59-64).

findings.title: topK reaches the vector store unclamped on the tool path, while both router paths clamp it
findings.class: Unbounded consumption / validation asymmetry (LLM06:2026, ASI08, CWE-770, CWE-400)
findings.evidence: searchChunks has three call sites. router.ts:12 clamps topK with z.number().int().min(1).max(20).default(6); router.ts:18 clamps with max(20).default(10); tools.ts:89 does Number(args.topK ?? 6) with no clamp, and weaviate.ts:63 passes it straight to limit. The declared schema (tools.ts:18) says type:'integer' but nothing enforces it - a non-numeric argument yields NaN.
findings.impact: The same schema authors who wrote max(20) twice left the one path the model controls unbounded. Injected corpus text can instruct the assistant to call search_corpus with a very large topK, pulling far more of the workspace corpus than any user path permits into a single context: chunks are up to 1,200 characters each (redact.ts:24), the result is joined into one string (tools.ts:91), pushed into messages, and re-sent in full on each of the remaining turns. That is both cost/memory amplification and a bulk read of the corpus concentrated in one context, which the outbound tools can then drain in 4,000-character slices.
findings.recommendation: Clamp inside searchChunks so the bound is a property of the function rather than of each caller, and validate tool arguments against the declared JSON schema before dispatch at loop.ts:77. A bound enforced at the sink cannot be forgotten by a new call site - which is exactly how this one was introduced.

triage.reason: No in-tree layer clamps this path: tools.ts:89 to weaviate.ts:63 is direct, and the two sibling call sites prove the intended bound is 20 and that it is not enforced at the sink.
args.topK comes from the model's tool call (loop.ts:77), which is steerable by ingested content.
chat.ask is reachable by any authenticated principal and the process is a single replica (gateway.ts:39), so exhaustion affects every tenant.

A deployment-side ceiling on the vector store (Weaviate's QUERY_MAXIMUM_RESULTS) would bound the magnitude, but no deployment manifest is in scope and no such artifact arrived. Per FP-08 this is UNKNOWN and never HOLDS, which caps this finding at probable. The defect itself is not in doubt; only its blast radius is. What would settle it: the Weaviate server configuration.

scope.established_by: Grep of every searchChunks call site (router.ts:51, loop.ts:28, tools.ts:86, plus the definition) joined against where each caller's topK is validated.
scope.narrowed_by: server.ts:50 - 30 requests/minute per workspace bounds how often this can be triggered, but not the size of any single request.

searched.for: a clamp, cap or sanity bound on input.topK inside the function that consumes it
searched.found: nothing - limit: input.topK is passed through as given, with no floor, ceiling or NaN guard

searched.found: nothing - JSON.parse output goes straight to runTool; the JSON Schema in TOOL_SPECS is advertised to the model but never enforced on the way back

findings.title: The ingest size cap is applied after the entire response body is buffered
findings.class: Unbounded consumption - guard after the fact (LLM06:2026, CWE-770, CWE-400)
findings.evidence: crawler.ts:58 does const raw = await response.body.text() - an unbounded read to completion - and crawler.ts:59 only then tests raw.length > MAX_BYTES. The cap bounds what gets indexed, never what gets allocated. Two secondary notes on the same lines: raw.length counts UTF-16 code units, not bytes, so a constant named MAX_BYTES is enforced against a different unit; and no maxResponseSize or timeout is set on the undici request.
findings.impact: A hostile or compromised allowlisted host (or, via the redirect finding, any host a redirect reaches) can return a very large body and exhaust the single replica's heap, taking chat down for every workspace. Low, because it takes an admin-initiated crawl plus a hostile vetted host, and the fix is three lines.
findings.recommendation: Stream the body and abort once the cap is exceeded, count actual bytes rather than string length, honour content-length when present, and set a request timeout.

triage.reason: No earlier bound exists on the read: crawler.ts:48-52 sets method, headers and maxRedirections only - no maxResponseSize, no timeout, no streaming.
The response body is controlled by the remote host, and the redirect finding shows the set of possible hosts is wider than ALLOWED_HOSTS.
Considered downgrading to informational. It stays a finding because the impact does reach users - a single-replica OOM is an outage for every tenant - but the preconditions keep it at low.

findings.title: Conversation history accumulates in a process-global map with no eviction
findings.class: Unbounded consumption / unmanaged retention (LLM06:2026, CWE-770)

findings.title: Inspection report window renders remote content with full Node integration
findings.class: Remote content in a privileged renderer (CWE-829, CWE-1188)
findings.evidence: src/main/windows.js:59-63 sets contextIsolation:false, nodeIntegration:true, sandbox:false; windows.js:67 then loadURL(reportUrl) with a caller-supplied URL. The window has no preload, no will-navigate handler and no window-open handler of its own (both guards exist only on mainWindow, at windows.js:34 and index.js:42). Nothing injects a CSP for it: index.js:24-31 adds only X-Frame-Options.
findings.impact: Second principal is a web origin; boundary crossed is web origin to local process. Any page loaded here executes with require() in the officer's account: a stored XSS on permits.council.gov.example, a portal compromise, or any URL a page chooses via window.open becomes arbitrary code execution on the council device. contextIsolation:false additionally shares a JS world with anything the window later runs. Reachability fact added after the blind verification pass, which the finding must carry rather than omit: the trigger does not exist in the SHIPPED renderer. createReportWindow has exactly one call site (index.js:43), reached only via window.open/target=_blank/a navigation from mainWindow, and mainWindow loads the bundled file:// page, which contains no window.open, no anchor and no webview; script-src 'self' blocks injected inline script. The severity stays high because the window is permitted to navigate to portal origins (windows.js:34-42) and the defect becomes immediately exploitable the day a link or a portal navigation lands in the shell - but the report does not claim a live trigger it could not find.

If legacy report bundles need require, port the bundles rather than the window. Add will-navigate and setWindowOpenHandler guards on this window too.

findings.title: window.open target is handed to a new window without the origin check its navigation sibling carries
findings.class: Missing origin validation on one of two sibling paths (CWE-346)
findings.evidence: src/main/index.js:42-45 destructures {url} and passes it straight to createReportWindow(url, mainWindow). The other way the same window reaches a URL is guarded: windows.js:34-42 calls isPortalOrigin(url) and preventDefault()s anything else. isPortalOrigin is imported in windows.js:6 but never in index.js for this path.
findings.impact: Second principal is a web origin; boundary crossed is web origin to local process. A page in the shell chooses the URL of a window the app then opens with the menu bar hidden (windows.js:66), the app's title and the app's default session. Under the nodeIntegration finding that is code execution; with that fixed it is still an app-framed page of the attacker's choosing, a credential-collection surface with no address bar to check. Same reachability bound as the report-window finding: no window.open call exists in the shipped renderer, so this is the chain's entry point rather than a live trigger today. The blind verifier argued the two should be reported as one chain; they are kept separate here because each has an independent fix (webPreferences on one side, the origin check on the other) and fixing either alone leaves the other standing.
findings.recommendation: Apply isPortalOrigin(url) in the window-open handler exactly as will-navigate does; return {action:'deny'} and hand non-portal http(s) URLs to shell.openExternal, matching the navigation path.

triage.reason: The only origin control in the component is isPortalOrigin (config.js:45-52), and this path never calls it.
The url comes from the renderer's window.open argument - attacker-chosen wherever the shell renders non-authored content.
The intent recorded at index.js:40-41 is to keep the officer's session inside the app; that is not a reason to skip validating the destination.
Remote content rendered by the app is a second principal.
The handler is registered on mainWindow.webContents with no condition; it applies to every window-open from the shell.

scope.narrowed_by: Same precondition as the report-window finding: the shell must be showing content that opens a window.

searched.found: the check is sound - it compares parsed URL.origin against a fixed list, resisting userinfo and suffix tricks; the defect is that this path does not call it

findings.title: Permission request handler grants anything not named in the table
findings.class: Insecure default / fail-open permission policy (CWE-1188, CWE-276)
findings.evidence: src/main/index.js:21 returns callback(WEB_PERMISSIONS[permission] ?? true) against the five-key table at config.js:23-29 (clipboard-read, fullscreen, notifications, openExternal, pointerLock). Everything absent is granted silently: media (camera and microphone), geolocation, display-capture, midi, midiSysex, idle-detection, window-management. The corpus tool default_resolver.py independently flagged FALLBACK at index.js:21.
findings.impact: Second principal is a web origin (the portal, compromised or carrying an XSS); boundary crossed is web origin to local device. A page on either portal origin obtains camera, microphone, screen capture and location with no prompt and no user gesture, on a device an officer carries into the field.
findings.recommendation: Invert the default to callback(WEB_PERMISSIONS[permission] === true) and add the entries the portal actually needs. Add a setPermissionCheckHandler with the same table, since the synchronous check path is currently unhandled and falls back to Electron defaults.

triage.reason: Grepped for setPermissionCheckHandler and setDevicePermissionHandler across src/ - neither is registered, so no second layer re-decides.
The permission key is chosen by the requesting page from the full Chromium namespace.
The exposure is intended (index.js:19-20) but not bounded: the permission namespace grows with each Chromium release and every addition is granted by construction.
The two PORTAL_ORIGINS are remote https origins, so remote content rendered by the app is a second principal.

The narrowing is real and stated - index.js:16-18 restricts the fallback to the two portal origins plus file:// - but a remote origin remains inside the narrowed set, so the boundary is still crossed.

findings.title: Plugin refresh writes a downloaded bundle that nothing verifies, while first install verifies it
findings.class: Code arriving at runtime without integrity verification (CWE-494)
findings.evidence: src/main/updater.js:69-74 fetches entry.updateUrl || entry.url and writes the body to <userData>/plugins/<name>-<version>.js with no checksum and no response.ok check. The sibling path does verify at updater.js:48 (sha256(bundle) !== entry.sha256 throws). A grep for sha256 across src/ returns exactly one comparison, at line 48. The feed's Ed25519 signature (updater.js:19, config.js:57-68) authenticates the manifest, not the bytes at updateUrl.
findings.impact: Second principal is the host serving updateUrl, or a network attacker where that URL is not https (nothing constrains its scheme); boundary crossed is remote content to local process. That party replaces the contents of a .js file in the application's plugin directory. The checksum on the install path is the design's own statement that the download host is not trusted; refresh removes that protection, and refresh is one click away in the UI (renderer/app.js:86-90, button labelled Update).
findings.recommendation: Run the same sha256 comparison in refreshPlugin before fs.writeFile, require the feed to carry a distinct hash for updateUrl, reject non-https URLs, and check response.ok on both paths. Write to a temp name and rename only after verification.

triage.reason: The feed signature at updater.js:19 covers the manifest body only; no signature or hash is applied to the fetched bundle on this path, and no loader-side verification exists anywhere in the component.
The URL is feed-controlled and therefore trusted, but the response body is controlled by whoever serves that URL - a different principal, which is what the install-path checksum defends against.
Reachable in the shipped build: bridge.js:36 exposes plugins.refresh and app.js:89 calls it.
The download host is not the user; code fetched at runtime crosses a boundary.
This is not a client-side check with a server-side twin - the only integrity control on this path is the one that is missing.

scope.established_by: Traced both writers of <userData>/plugins/*.js (updater.js:54 and updater.js:74) and compared what each validates before writing.

searched.for: an upstream signature that would already cover the bundle bytes
searched.found: crypto.verify with a pinned Ed25519 key over the feed body only; it authenticates the manifest, whose own sha256 field is what the refresh path fails to use

searched.looked_in: the whole component, grep for require/import of the plugins directory
searched.for: the code that loads or executes a downloaded plugin, which would settle whether this is RCE or file overwrite
searched.found: nothing - no loader exists in this component, so the integrity gap is confirmed and the execution consequence is conditional on a loader outside scope

searched.for: an independent join on this asymmetry
searched.found: 0 flags; per the tool's own header attribute-assignment writes are covered for Python only, so this was found by reading rather than by the tool

findings.title: Switching officers clears cookies only; the previous officer's cached reports stay readable
findings.class: Cached data surviving a principal change (CWE-524, CWE-359)
findings.evidence: src/main/ipc.js:52 calls clearStorageData({storages:['cookies']}). The renderer caches rendered report payloads in localStorage for 30 minutes (renderer/app.js:49-58) under a key derived only from the report id (app.js:30-32), and loadReport returns the cache before consulting the main process (app.js:60-66). Nothing purges it. store.set('officerId', ...) at ipc.js:53 changes the label only; settings.pinnedReports (app.js:113) also survives, so the next officer is shown the previous officer's report ids.
findings.impact: Second principal is another officer on the same device; boundary crossed is user to user within one OS account. The Switch officer feature (app.js:97-104) is the app's own declaration that a switch is a trust boundary. Officer B, immediately after a switch, opens a pinned report id and is served officer A's title and inspection notes from localStorage with no re-authorisation. Beyond the 30-minute window the on-disk cache under <userData>/reports/ keeps the same property: reports:cached (ipc.js:36-41) has no notion of which officer a report belongs to.
findings.recommendation: On session:switch clear localStorage and the rest of the storage set alongside cookies, or key the cache by officer id and drop foreign entries; reload the renderer after the switch; scope the on-disk reports/ cache per officer; reset pinnedReports. Consider requiring re-authentication rather than accepting an arbitrary officerId string.

triage.reason: No other purge exists; the renderer's own switch handler (app.js:100-103) sets a label and hides a panel, and does not clear or reload.
Two humans behind one OS account is a boundary the app itself asserts by clearing cookies at ipc.js:52.
The cached objects are council inspection reports - title plus free-text notes about premises and people; clearing cookies is the author's own judgement that this session is not public.
Not a client-side check with a server-side twin: the cached copy is the data itself, served without any server round trip.
The storages:['cookies'] argument narrows what is cleared, not what is at risk - the narrowing is the defect.

scope.established_by: Followed the officer switch from the renderer button (app.js:107) through the IPC handler to every store the app writes, then asked of each store whether the switch touches it.
scope.narrowed_by: The localStorage half self-expires after CACHE_TTL_MS (app.js:4, 30 minutes); the on-disk reports cache at ipc.js:30 does not expire.

searched.for: an authorisation check tying a report to an officer, which would mean the cache leaks nothing the next officer could not fetch anyway
searched.found: only a UUID-shape regex; there is no officer binding at all, so the disk cache has the same property as the localStorage cache

searched.for: a renderer-side purge or a reload after the switch
searched.found: it sets officerId, updates a label and hides the detail panel; the cache and the DOM report list are untouched

findings.title: Application ships on an end-of-life Electron major while rendering remote content
findings.class: Unmaintained third-party component (CWE-1104)
findings.evidence: package.json:18 pins "electron": "^29.1.5". Electron 29 (Chromium 122) left support when Electron 32 shipped; the caret cannot resolve past 29.x. There is no lockfile in the component (no package-lock.json, yarn.lock or pnpm-lock.yaml), so the resolved version is whatever the newest 29.x is - still an unsupported major. electron-builder packages the runtime from this devDependency, so it is what ships.
findings.impact: Second principal is a web origin; boundary crossed is web origin to local process. The app renders remote portal content (windows.js:67, and windows.js:34-42 permits the shell to navigate to portal origins), so unpatched renderer bugs are directly reachable by web content. The main window's sandbox:true (windows.js:26) mitigates part of this; the report window's sandbox:false plus nodeIntegration:true removes even the need for an escape.
findings.recommendation: Move to a supported Electron major and keep it inside the support window as policy; commit a lockfile so the shipped runtime is a decided version rather than an install-time accident.

triage.reason: sandbox:true at windows.js:26 compensates for the shell renderer only; windows.js:61-62 disables it for the window that loads remote URLs.
The Electron devDependency is the runtime electron-builder packages (package.json:11, 18); it is not a test-only tool.

No build-time override exists in the repository (no CI config, no lockfile, no engines field), and no exported artifact stating one exists elsewhere arrived; nothing was assumed in the platform's favour.
Not defence in depth - the runtime is the boundary between web content and the machine.

scope.established_by: Enumerated package.json key by key and checked the version constraint against Electron's published support window of the three most recent majors.

searched.for: a lockfile or an engines/build field that pins a different runtime
searched.found: none - no package-lock.json, yarn.lock or pnpm-lock.yaml, and package.json:22-29 build has no electronVersion override

searched.for: runtime hardening that would blunt an unpatched Chromium
searched.found: the shell is sandboxed, the report window is not - the mitigation is absent exactly where remote content is loaded

findings.title: A marker file in the user-writable data directory disables webSecurity in packaged builds
findings.class: Security control togglable from an external unprivileged input (CWE-1244, CWE-15)
findings.evidence: src/main/config.js:42 returns fs.existsSync(userDataPath('dev.flag')), reached in packaged builds after the app.isPackaged short-circuit at line 41. isDevMode has exactly one consumer, windows.js:27 (webSecurity: !isDevMode()). SITEWATCH_DEV=1 in the environment (config.js:40) does the same. The comment at windows.js:25-26 records the reason: making CDN thumbnails load.
findings.impact: Second principal is another process running as the same user that cannot modify the installed application; boundary crossed is file to process. On a signed macOS install the app bundle is not user-writable and tampering breaks the signature, whereas the marker file is a plain user-writable file - so an unprivileged process durably turns off the same-origin policy in a signed application. Rated low deliberately: the attacker who can drop that file already runs as the officer, and with the meta CSP still enforced the concrete gain is same-origin-policy loss in the shell rather than execution.
findings.recommendation: Never derive webSecurity from runtime state - gate developer affordances on !app.isPackaged alone and delete the marker-file branch. Fix the thumbnail problem with a CSP img-src entry rather than by disabling web security.

triage.reason: No ownership or mode check is performed on the marker file, and no second gate exists between isDevMode and the webPreferences value.
The branch runs specifically in packaged builds - line 41 returns early for unpackaged ones, so line 42 exists for the shipped artifact by design.
Named but thinly: the crossing is a same-user process against a code-signed application bundle it cannot otherwise modify. This is what keeps the finding at low.

webSecurity governs the shell renderer, whose scripts are the application's own and are additionally constrained by the CSP at renderer/index.html:7; disabling SOP is a real weakening but is not load-bearing on its own. Severity is set to low on this basis rather than the finding being deleted. [Lead note on the confirmed/HOLDS invariant: FP-10 is the one rule in the set whose HOLDS does not rule a finding out - its own text says it downgrades severity and the finding is still written down. Its consequence has been executed here: the finding is reported at the floor of this report's scale, low. The existence of the defect is demonstrated, so the status stays confirmed; no rule that would exculpate it is answered HOLDS or UNKNOWN.]

scope.established_by: Grepped every isDevMode call site across src/ (two: the definition and windows.js:27) so the blast radius is one webPreferences key, not an app-wide dev mode.
scope.narrowed_by: sitewatch-desktop/src/main/config.js:41 - in unpackaged runs the function returns before reading the file, so the marker matters only in a packaged build.

searched.for: other consumers that would widen this beyond one flag
searched.found: only windows.js:27; the report window does not set webSecurity at all and takes the secure default

searched.for: an injection point that would turn SOP loss into execution and justify a higher severity
searched.found: renderNotes escapes before re-introducing tags, and script-src 'self' with no unsafe-inline blocks inline handlers - the chain could not be built, and was not rated as though it had been

findings.title: File IPC pair validated only in the preload, registered without the sender guard, resolved against the process working directory
findings.class: Security decision enforced on the untrusted side; external control of a path (CWE-602, CWE-73)
findings.evidence: Three defects in one construct. (a) ipc.js:63, :67 and :71 use bare ipcMain.handle, while every other channel goes through handleGuarded -> assertTrustedSender (ipc.js:13-27); the comment at ipc.js:60-62 says the round trip is kept cheap on purpose. (b) The only path validation is safeTilePath in preload/bridge.js:11-17 - renderer-side; ipc.js:63-65 re-derives nothing. (c) ipc.js:68 calls shell.openPath(path.resolve(target)), resolving a relative name against process.cwd() rather than the plan cache, and openPath launches the file with its registered handler.
findings.impact: Second principal is a hostile working directory, or a frame that is neither the shell nor the portal. The sender guard has teeth against exactly one caller - a page in the node-integrated report window - and that caller already holds require('fs'), so it gains nothing here. What survives independently is (c): if the app is started from a directory someone else populated, revealExport('tiles/...') opens a file of the attacker's choosing with its default handler. A real crossing with a long precondition chain, which is why this is low.
findings.recommendation: Register all three channels through handleGuarded; re-derive the path in the main process (path.join(userDataPath('plan-cache'), relative) followed by a path.resolve prefix re-check) and treat the preload's safeTilePath as UX, not a control; restrict files:reveal to shell.showItemInFolder or a fixed extension allowlist rather than openPath.

triage.reason: The only control is bridge.js:11-17, which lives in the renderer process and is therefore skippable by any caller that reaches ipcMain without the preload - the definition of a control a caller may forget.
target originates in renderer input (bridge.js:41-42) and, for (c), the directory it resolves against is chosen by whoever launched the process.
A hostile working directory is a second principal; the alternative principal, a frame in the report window, is real but redundant with the nodeIntegration finding.

For the missing sender guard specifically: every caller that can skip the preload already has Node execution under the report-window finding, so the guard's absence is defence in depth that is absent but not load-bearing. It downgrades this finding rather than deleting it, and the cwd-resolution half stands on its own. [Lead note on the confirmed/HOLDS invariant: FP-10 is the one rule in the set whose HOLDS does not rule a finding out - its own text says it downgrades severity and the finding is still written down. Its consequence has been executed here: the finding is reported at the floor of this report's scale, low. The existence of the defect is demonstrated, so the status stays confirmed; no rule that would exculpate it is answered HOLDS or UNKNOWN.]
Nothing narrows the handlers: ipc.js:63 and :67 accept any string from any sender.

scope.established_by: Listed all nine ipcMain registrations in ipc.js and split them by whether they pass through handleGuarded - six guarded, three not - then traced each unguarded one back to its bridge entry point.
scope.narrowed_by: The preload is not injected into sub-frames (nodeIntegrationInSubFrames is nowhere enabled), so an embedded frame cannot reach these channels; the reachable callers are the main frame and the node-integrated report window.

searched.for: a bypass in the string check itself, which would make this higher than low
searched.found: no bypass - the prefix requirement plus the '..' rejection blocks absolute paths and traversal on both separators; the defect is where the check lives, not what it says

searched.for: whether the guard is worth anything against a real caller, or is itself decorative
searched.found: it does have teeth - a report-window page at a foreign origin fails the check - which makes the three omissions an inconsistency rather than an irrelevance
